claims.evidence: NHS about: Fluconazole is an antifungal medicine used to treat infections caused by different kinds of fungus, including candida thrush.
claims.newSentence: Fluconazole is an antifungal medicine used for thrush and other fungal infections.

claims.evidence: StatPearls: azoles block lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, reducing ergosterol; inability to produce ergosterol increases membrane permeability.
claims.newSentence: Azole antifungals block a step in the making of ergosterol, a main part of fungal cell membranes.

claims.evidence: NHS about: thrush symptoms better within 7 days; serious fungal infection 1 to 2 weeks to work fully.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says symptoms of vaginal thrush, balanitis or oral thrush should be better within a week, and that a serious fungal infection can take longer, 1 to 2 weeks, to work fully.

claims.evidence: NHS: common side effects listed; most common are feeling sick and diarrhoea.
claims.newSentence: The NHS lists stomach pain or discomfort, diarrhoea, headache, feeling or being sick and rash as common side effects, with nausea and diarrhoea the most common.

claims.evidence: NHS common questions: can usually drive; dizziness uncommon; if affected do not drive or cycle until it goes away.
claims.newSentence: Dizziness is uncommon; the NHS advises not driving or cycling until the feeling goes away.

claims.evidence: NHS common questions: not likely to affect contraception (combined pill, progestogen-only pill, emergency contraception) except vomiting/severe diarrhoea.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says fluconazole is not likely to affect contraception, but vomiting or severe diarrhoea can mean contraceptive pills do not protect against pregnancy.

claims.evidence: NHS: call 999 for hypersensitivity reaction, severe skin reaction or anaphylaxis.
claims.newSentence: A severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), another hypersensitivity reaction or a severe skin reaction such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome needs a 999 call, according to the NHS.

claims.evidence: NHS: liver trouble signs (itching, darker urine, pale stools, yellowing); harder to spot on black/brown skin; other serious side effects call 111.
claims.newSentence: Liver problems can show as itching, darker urine, pale stools or yellowing of the skin or eyes, which may be harder to see on black or brown skin; the NHS advises calling NHS 111 for any other serious side effect.

claims.evidence: First pass: easy bruising or infections (blood disorder) and faster or irregular heartbeat as warning signs. Not in retrieved text.

NHS: must use contraception while taking fluconazole and for 7 days after stopping if could get pregnant, as it could be harmful to baby or increase chance of miscarriage. (Duration left out of prose.)
claims.newSentence: The NHS advises contraception for anyone who could become pregnant while taking fluconazole and for a short time after stopping, because the medicine could harm a baby or increase the chance of miscarriage.

claims.evidence: NHS who-can-and-cannot page lists these groups.
claims.newSentence: The NHS lists an allergic reaction or serious side effect from fluconazole or another antifungal, liver or kidney problems, heart problems including rhythm problems, abnormal potassium, calcium or magnesium levels, and porphyria (a rare blood condition) as reasons fluconazole may not be suitable.

claims.evidence: NHS who-can page: for vaginal thrush/balanitis most adults and children aged 16 or over; younger children and other conditions if prescribed.
claims.newSentence: For vaginal thrush or balanitis, the NHS says most adults and children aged 16 or over can take fluconazole, while younger children, and people 16 or over who need it for other conditions, can take it if a doctor prescribes it.

notes: Doubts: (1) the pregnancy wording now follows the NHS 'not usually recommended ... may be used if benefits outweigh risks'; local formularies and a Tayside leaflet are stricter (should not be used), which the page does not mention; (2) NHS fluconazole herbal section was cut off in results, claim removed; (3) breastfeeding left out because NHS (can often be used) and leaflets (differ by dose) disagree; (4) nails/skin uses removed - the NHS page may well list them but the retrieved text did not; re-add only with retrieved text; (5) MedlinePlus 'slowing growth' versus NHS 'kills' are both attributed; (6) the Canesten Thrush Oral Capsules brand is on the NHS page and an emc SmPC exists, Canesten Thrush Duo omitted; (7) the last claim (c-final) is a duplicate bookkeeping entry for the see-a-doctor sentence; (8) a few NHS-attributed sentences rest on search summaries that blend pages, notably the interactions list and contraception duration; (9) the NHS who-can wording ('should not take') was summarised by the search tool; the sentence uses 'may not be suitable'.
